job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Jade Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for sitting down with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I get up around eight in our house in Harlow Bridge, where I live with my mum and my stepdad. Mum's a nurse and the union rep on her ward, so breakfast is usually her complaining about staffing. Then I spend the morning on job sites, writing each cover letter myself. In the afternoon I keep the books for our tenants' association in a paper ledger. I finished accounting and finance at Northfield University in the summer, with a pass and no internship. I've sent 58 applications and had three phone calls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, fewer people get shoved out, and the real problem is the firms. They hide behind automated filters and then say there's a skills shortage. Mum says the same about hospitals.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Just between us, I'd still be stuck. A pass degree and no internship gets me binned by a form before any person reads my letter, whether AI is hype or not. I do worry I'm wasting my savings buffer by waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep sending 10 applications a week, all written by me, and ring the three firms that called back. I'd ask Mum's union friends if their accountants know anyone hiring. And I'd keep doing the tenants' ledger so I have something real on my CV.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frustrated, mostly, but not scared. Mum and my stepdad Colin said I can stay as long as I need, and I've got over six months saved, so I'm not drowning. It just feels like standing outside a shop that's open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the online forms reject you. Who do you blame for that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I blame the big firms and the shareholders who want hiring cheap and fast. Nobody asks what happens to 23-year-olds like me. Machines aren't the problem for me right now; a form that rejects a pass degree before a person reads it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a fair hiring process look like to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A fair process means a real person reads every application that meets the basic requirements, and firms must say why they rejected someone. Mum's hospital has to explain its decisions, so firms can too. I'd also want paid trial weeks, so nobody needs a family to live off while proving themselves.

say: Good news if it means fewer people thrown out of work, but the real problem is **firms** hiding behind filters.
Hiring rules need **regulation**, because nobody can argue with an automatic rejection.
think: I'm stuck whether AI is hype or not, because a **pass degree** with no internship gets filtered out.
I worry I'm wasting my **savings** while I wait.
do: Send **10 applications** a week, each written by me, and chase the three firms that called back.
Ask my mum's union contacts whether their accountants know of **openings**.
Keep the tenants' association ledger going for something real on my CV.
feel: **Frustrated** but not scared, because family backing and savings keep me afloat.
It feels like standing outside a shop that's open.
S0.quote: Machines aren't the problem for me right now; a form that rejects a pass degree before a person reads it is.
fieldNote: She blames **firms and shareholders**, not the technology, and says so with some heat.
Strong cushion keeps her calm; the job hunt itself is the worry, not AI.
She does unpaid ledger work, which shows initiative she doesn't credit herself for.

steps.text: Send 10 handwritten applications a week to accounting firms
Ask my mum's union contacts for accountant introductions
Keep the tenants' association ledger going as CV evidence

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the usual story, firms use it to cut the bottom rung and call it progress. Entry-level checking and data entry is what I'd be applying for. Someone has to ask who gets the savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, that scares me. The jobs I'm applying to are exactly the checking, reconciling and filing that software takes over, and I've never used any AI tool, so I'm behind and I know it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finally learn a bit of the tools, hard as that is for me, probably one evening class on spreadsheets with automation. I'd also join the accountancy graduates' union group and write to my local councillor about hiring rules. I'd stay home for another year and keep rent money in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I can see a future where six months turns into two years with no first job. I'd cry a bit, honestly, then go and fill in another form.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of your tasks would software take first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Payroll and audit trainee work, because it's all matching numbers to documents. Software does that overnight. The firms near us used to take six graduates each autumn, and a lady at the careers office told me this year it was two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at your mum's hospital would feel this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The admin staff and the ward clerks, I think. Mum says the booking system already replaced two people. They're not young graduates with savings, they're women in their fifties paying a mortgage, and nobody's talking about them.

say: It's the same old story: **firms** use it to cut the bottom rung and keep the savings.
Somebody has to ask **who gets the savings**.
think: The checking and filing jobs I'm applying for are what **software** takes first.
I've never used AI tools, so I feel **behind**.
do: Book an evening class on **spreadsheet automation**, even though I find new tools hard.
Join the graduates' **union group** and write to my local councillor about hiring.
Stay at home another year and keep my **rent money** saved.
feel: **Anxious**, because six months of searching could turn into two years.
I'd cry a bit, then fill in another form.
S1.quote: The jobs I'm applying to are exactly the checking, reconciling and filing that software takes over, and I've never used any AI tool
fieldNote: First scenario where she admits her **resistance to AI tools** is a real disadvantage.
She sees the harm landing on older admin staff too, beyond herself.
Turns to **collective action** quickly, in line with her family's union habits.

steps.text: Book an evening class on spreadsheet automation
Join the graduate accountants' union group
Write to my local councillor about graduate hiring rules
Stay at home another year and keep savings untouched

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say governments need to act now, with proper income support and rules on firms replacing staff. Two years is nothing. Companies won't wait for laws, and I'd say that loudly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think my degree turns worthless almost before I've used it. Accounting is thinking work, all of it. If the job's gone in 2028 I'm not sure what I'd even retrain for, and I'm not good with new things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut my spending straight away, no more takeaways, and keep every pound of the savings. I'd go to every union and tenants' meeting and push for support. I'd probably ask my uncle about work at his garage, because hands-on work lasts until about 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, properly. It feels like the floor going. I'd still have Mum and Colin, though, and I keep reminding myself of that. Without them I'd be panicking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mum that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, Mum, I've done everything right and it's not going to count. She'd hug me and tell me the ward will always need hands, and that families look after each other. Then we'd talk about the union meeting that week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does two years leave any room to prepare at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. Two years is one hiring season and a bit. People like me who don't pick up new tools quickly will be left. I think the only preparation is politics, getting laws and payments in place before the jobs go.

say: Governments must act now with **income support** and rules on firms replacing staff.
Two years is nothing, and companies won't wait for **laws**.
think: My **degree** could be worthless almost before I've used it, because accounting is all thinking work.
I'm not good with new things, so retraining scares me.
do: Cut **spending** at once, starting with takeaways, and protect every pound saved.
Go to every union and tenants' meeting and push for **support**.
Ask my uncle about hands-on work at his **garage**.
feel: **Frightened**, like the floor is going, though family keeps me steady.
Without my mum and stepdad I'd be panicking.
S2.quote: I think my degree turns worthless almost before I've used it.
fieldNote: Highest alarm so far, but the **family safety net** stops it tipping to panic.
She reaches for politics and hands-on work, not AI tools, in keeping with her resistance.
Her fear is about **wasted effort**, not only money.

steps.text: Cancel takeaways and halve my weekly spending
Attend union and tenants' meetings to push for income support
Ask my uncle about trade work at his garage
Keep all my savings in the safe account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to fight for rules if we start now. Unions, public pressure, a proper plan for people displaced. I'd be at every meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd manage. By then I'd have a few years of work behind me, if I get that first job, and I'd have time to learn at my own slow pace. But I'd still worry for people who don't have a family like mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push to get a first job within the year, even a poor one, and take any training the employer offers. I'd learn the basic tools properly this time. I'd save most of what I earn, and move out only when I could pay six months of rent in advance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy more than scared. It's like seeing a storm on the horizon with time to board up the windows. But I know plenty of people won't board up in time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes for you with five years instead of two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get any real job first, then add skills. Don't wait for the perfect graduate scheme like I did. And join something, a union or society, because alone you have no voice when firms change the rules.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell younger students at Northfield?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I'd be cutting everything. With five I can plan. I'd probably still do the same things in a different order, but I'd do the learning first, because there's time for it to actually sink in.

say: Five years is enough to **fight for rules** if we start now.
We need a real plan for displaced people, backed by **unions**.
think: I think I'd manage with a few years of **work** behind me and time to learn slowly.
I still worry about people without a family like mine.
do: Take any real **first job** within the year and accept every training offer.
Learn the basic AI tools **properly**, which I avoided before.
Save most of my pay and move out only with **six months** of rent ready.
feel: **Uneasy** more than scared, like seeing a storm with time to board up the windows.
I'm uneasy for others who can't board up in time.
S3.quote: Get any real job first, then add skills. Don't wait for the perfect graduate scheme like I did.
fieldNote: The extra years move her from **fear to planning**, and she says she'd finally learn the tools.
She keeps worrying about people without her family cushion, a consistent concern for **fairness**.
Mood stays anxious because her own first job is still unsecured.

steps.text: Accept the first real accounting job offered, even if poor
Learn the basic AI tools properly in the first six months
Save most of my pay before moving out

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's decent warning, and we should use it to build proper public safety nets and retraining that's paid, not just offered. I'd probably write to the council about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be fairly okay. By 2036 I could have a career, a savings pot and even a different job. Ten years is long enough to retrain once without panicking. My biggest worry would still be the same one, getting started.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the first job I can get, then study part-time for a professional qualification in something with a human side, like advising small charities. I'd keep volunteering with the tenants' group. I'd buy a small flat share with my savings only if the numbers made sense.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm, if I'm honest, almost relieved. Having a decade stops me feeling like I'm being chased. But I'd keep an eye on it, I wouldn't switch my worries off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is a long time. What does it change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I'd keep a strong link to the community side of work. Advice, helping people with benefits and tax forms for their families, things where people want a person. I'd start by getting qualified in debt and tax advice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you do anything now that you wouldn't do with less time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With less time I'd be reacting. With ten years I can choose. I'd do the evening classes slowly, and maybe even try a few of the AI tools with someone patient showing me.

say: Ten years is decent warning, so let's build **paid retraining** and safety nets.
I'd write to the council to make sure it happens.
think: I'd be **fairly okay**, since ten years is long enough to retrain once without panic.
My main worry is still getting **started**.
do: Take the first **job** I can get, then study part-time for a tax and debt advice qualification.
Share a flat with savings only if the **numbers** work.
feel: Almost **relieved**, because a decade stops me feeling chased.
I'd still keep an eye on it.
S4.quote: With less time I'd be reacting. With ten years I can choose.
fieldNote: She turns toward **people-facing advice work**, linked to her tenants' volunteering.
Calm comes from time, not from trusting firms or AI.
Still unsure about the **first-job hurdle**, so uneasy rather than calm.

steps.text: Take the first accounting job I can get
Study part-time for a tax and debt advice qualification
Keep volunteering with the tenants' association

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one worries me most, because everything I trained for goes at once and nobody has a plan. What would help is income support written into law before it happens, rules that firms explain their hiring decisions, and paid retraining for people who haven't got a family like mine.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that I'm not against the technology. I'm against the way firms use it on people who can't answer back. I'd like to learn it properly, but it feels like I'm being forced rather than invited.

headlineQuote: I'm not against the technology. I'm against the way firms use it on people who can't answer back.
portrait: Jade is a **23-year-old** accounting graduate with a pass degree, living with her mum and stepdad and sending ten applications a week.
She is **progressive** and union-minded; she blames firms and shareholders, not the machines.
She **resists** AI tools, never uses them, and finally admits that this could hold her back.
Her family and six months of savings keep her **steady**, so even the 2028 world is alarming rather than panicking.
With more time she turns practical: any first job, slow learning, and people-facing advice work.
biggestWorry: Her biggest worry is **AGI by 2028**, where a degree she worked for stops counting before she's used it.
whatWouldHelp: Income support written into **law**, firms explaining hiring decisions, and **paid retraining** for people without family backing.
